source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Framework: each agent has a perspective (how it encodes solutions) and a heuristic (how it searches). A team can only get stuck at a point that is a local optimum for every member, whatever the team procedure.
numbers: Model only; no human data. Perspective = mapping M from solutions to internal language; heuristic = mapping A from internal language to subsets of solutions.
quote: a group of agents can get stuck only at a solution that lies in the intersection of the individual agents' local optima
limits: Formal idealisation. Authors say communication and learning are left out.
agent_relevance: Defines team diversity as differences in search maps, a usable idea for an LLM team: diversity means different failure points.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Computational experiment: random value function on a ring; agents differ only in heuristic. A random team beat a team of the individually best agents.
numbers: Ring of n=2000 points, values uniform on [0,100]; heuristic = k=3 ordered step sizes up to l=12 or 20; tried l 6-20, k 2-7, n 200-10000. Single run l=12: best agent 87.3, worst 84.3; 10 best average 87.1; 10 random average 85.6; group of 10 best 93.2 (diversity 0.72); group of 10 random 94.7 (diversity 0.92).
limits: Single illustrative run in text; the full result is the 50-trial table (next line). Agents differ only in heuristic, not perspective.
agent_relevance: Direct template for testing 'diverse mediocre beats clones of best' with LLM samples.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Table 1 (50 trials). Random teams beat best-ability teams in every cell, but the gap shrinks when the team gets bigger.
numbers: 10 agents, l=12: best 92.56 (sd .020) diversity 70.98%; random 94.53 (sd .007) diversity 90.99%. 20 agents, l=12: best 93.78 vs random 94.72 (diversity 74.95% vs 91.46%). 10 agents, l=20 (6,840 heuristics): best 93.52 vs random 96.08 (diversity 73.69% vs 94.31%).
limits: Pool is finite and fixed, so with 20 agents the best group becomes more diverse. Gaps are about 1 to 2.5 points on a 0-100 scale.
agent_relevance: The advantage is modest and depends on pool size and on how many agents are used.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Theorem: with probability one, for large enough pools, N1 random agents beat the N1 individually best of N drawn agents. Needs four assumptions: agents are intelligent (find a weakly better point), problem is hard (no agent always finds the optimum), agents are diverse (for every non-optimal point some agent can improve), and the best agent is unique.
numbers: Finite-X proof; in it the best group is shown to be made of identical agents. Authors call that an artefact of the finite version.
quote: as the pool of problem solvers grows larger, the very best problem solvers must become similar
limits: Later critics (Thompson, a21) say the assumptions are strong and the result near-trivial. Authors admit the random group must be large for the result to hold.
agent_relevance: Warns that picking top-k by individual score produces correlated errors. Fits our guardrail on correlated errors.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Authors' own limits and a design hint: teams should mix similar perspectives (cheap to communicate) with diverse heuristics. The value of an agent depends on the others, not only on its own ability.
numbers: Argument in concluding remarks; no numbers.
limits: Model has no communication or learning; later work (a15) adds communication error.
agent_relevance: Suggests picking team members by how differently they fail, not by solo score.

source: Fazelpour and Steel (2022) Diversity, Trust, and Conformity: A Simulation Study, Philosophy of Science 89(2):209-231
finding: Extends Zollman's bandit network model with two social groups. Tests whether demographic diversity helps even when it carries no task knowledge, by cutting uncritical trust and conformity.
numbers: Two-armed bandit, option A pays 0.5 and B 0.501; 10,000 runs of 3,000 experiments of 1,000 tries; greedy Bayesian (Beta) agents; success = unanimous correct consensus; networks: complete, cycle, wheel.
limits: Simulation only, abstract agents; the authors warn it is not advice to sow distrust in teams.
agent_relevance: Shows the benefit of diversity can come from damping mutual influence, a design lever for multi-sample agents.

source: Fazelpour and Steel (2022) Diversity, Trust, and Conformity: A Simulation Study, Philosophy of Science 89(2):209-231
finding: Simulation 1: with out-group trust factor w, full distrust (w=0.005) was worst, and full trust (w=1) was second worst. Moderate distrust was best, mainly in complete networks. The benefit is largest when the two groups are near equal in size.
numbers: w between 0 and 1 applied to out-group data; compared complete, cycle and wheel networks; exact success probabilities appear only in Figures 2a-b (not read as numbers).
limits: Sparser networks (cycle, wheel) already do well, so distrust helps little there and slows convergence.
agent_relevance: Moderate damping of other samples' influence, not zero and not full, may beat naive sharing in an agent team.

source: Fazelpour and Steel (2022) Diversity, Trust, and Conformity: A Simulation Study, Philosophy of Science 89(2):209-231
finding: Simulation 2: conformity pressure hurts everyone. For low conformity kappa, mixed groups beat homogeneous ones; for higher kappa the order flips and homogeneous groups do better because of between-group polarisation.
numbers: Complete networks of 10 agents; kappa values 0, 0.00625, 0.0125, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1; Other-Total-Ratio rule. Homogeneous groups often reached a wrong public consensus while some agents privately disagreed.
limits: Benefit appears only at mild conformity. Agents are greedy; no status or power.
agent_relevance: Hidden dissent matters: make the agent surface minority answers instead of letting majority vote hide them.

source: Zollman (2010) The Epistemic Benefit of Transient Diversity, Erkenntnis 72:17-35
finding: Bandit-network model: a division of labor survives if information is limited or agents hold extreme beliefs. If both hold, diversity never ends and the group fails to converge. The goal is transient, not permanent, diversity.
numbers: Notes in page: each trial 1,000 pulls, success rates 0.5 vs 0.499; initial priors drawn on [0,4], and for the extreme-belief case alpha, beta from [0,7000]. Results qualitatively match Zollman (2007).
quote: the real epistemic goal is not diversity but transient diversity
limits: Only the abstract and footnotes were readable (paywall). Numbers beyond the notes are not verified here.
agent_relevance: Exploration should be time-limited: keep rival hypotheses alive early, then converge.

source: Zollman (2010) The Epistemic Benefit of Transient Diversity, Erkenntnis 72:17-35
finding: Case study in the page notes: the stomach-bacteria theory of ulcers was dismissed from 1954 to the 1980s after one flawed study; Zollman uses it as a historical case of premature consensus.
numbers: Dates: Palmer 1954; Warren and Marshall 1984 (Lancet) per the page notes; bismuth used for ulcers back to 1868.
limits: Single historical case, told by the author.
agent_relevance: Premature consensus on a wrong hypothesis is the failure to guard against.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese (author names as I recall them; not confirmed from the page text)
finding: Review of network-epistemology models. Less connected networks reach the correct consensus more often (Zollman 2007, 2010); tightly connected networks let one misleading result sway everyone. Gains come at the cost of slower consensus.
numbers: Cites March (1991) on NK landscapes and Lazer and Friedman (2007), Fang et al. (2010): less connected networks find better solutions but take longer. Zollman calls this a speed versus precision trade-off.
limits: Secondary source; numbers of the original studies not given.
agent_relevance: Information sharing between agent samples early can lock in a wrong answer; limit sharing until each has explored.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese (author names as I recall them; not confirmed from the page text)
finding: Review lists seven mechanisms that keep diversity of practice alive: low connectivity, stubbornness, confirmation bias, funders favouring risky science, inter-group distrust, proprietary industry research, testimonial injustice.
numbers: Gabriel and O'Connor (2021): mild confirmation bias helps, higher levels cause polarisation. Kummerfeld and Zollman (2015): exploration is a free-rider problem, so institutions must fund it. Wu (2022a): an ignored marginalised group learns better. Wu (2022b): a non-sharing group forms true beliefs faster.
limits: All are model results. Each mechanism also raises polarisation risk.
agent_relevance: Each mechanism is a candidate knob for an agent: set a diversity budget, not a free-for-all.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese (author names as I recall them; not confirmed from the page text)
finding: Costs of diversity: Rosenstock et al. (2017) argue Zollman's advice to cut communication is highly inefficient on hard problems, and on easy problems almost every community already succeeds. Too much diversity becomes stable polarisation, and propagandists can exploit disagreement.
numbers: Review cites decision-theory exploration rules (Gittins index, epsilon-greedy) as better exploration than blunt diversity.
limits: Review text; see a24 for the Rosenstock paper itself (not opened).
agent_relevance: Prefer principled explore-exploit rules (bandit style) over broad diversity when the budget is finite.

source: Karge (2025) When Diversity in Voting Trumps Ability, Episteme
finding: Derives exact conditions for diversity beating ability in a Condorcet jury voting model; diversity is modelled as the influence of an opinion leader on the voters. Notes the Hong-Page theorem has been criticised for mathematical rigour (Thompson 2014).
numbers: Gives probability bounds and a diversity threshold (formulas not read in full here).
quote: Despite considerable criticism regarding the DTA's mathematical rigor, it has sparked substantial interdisciplinary discussion.
limits: Voting setting, not search. Focus is formal conditions.
agent_relevance: For majority-vote ensembles, correlated voters (a leader) erase the gain from more voters.

source: Authors not recorded (2023) Does (mis)communication mitigate the upshot of diversity? (PMC10038257)
finding: Adds a noisy communication channel to the Hong-Page model. Diverse teams still tend to beat more expert but homogeneous teams. How much they gain depends on four interacting factors: problem complexity, number of approaches, ways of encoding the problem, and institutional search method.
numbers: Landscape of 2,000 positions on a ring, built on Singer's agent-based model; heuristic = n-tuples such as (1,11,4); miscommunication error can be correlated with agent difference.
limits: Relationships are non-linear and sometimes non-monotonic; team routines that cut miscommunication in one setting can amplify it in another.
agent_relevance: Diverse samples need a shared representation to pass answers; if each LLM encodes the problem differently, merging costs rise.

source: Authors not recorded (2023) Does (mis)communication mitigate the upshot of diversity? (PMC10038257)
finding: Small miscommunication can sometimes help, and a team routine that works in one setting can backfire in another.
numbers: Reported qualitatively in abstract and introduction.
limits: No single recommended routine.
agent_relevance: Test merge methods per task type; do not assume one aggregation rule fits all.

source: Longino (1990) Science as Social Knowledge; Longino (2002) The Fate of Knowledge
finding: Objectivity comes from community-level transformative criticism. Four norms: public venues for criticism, uptake of criticism, shared public standards, tempered equality of intellectual authority. Background assumptions become visible only when others with different assumptions challenge them.
numbers: No quantitative data (philosophical argument). Crossref lists about 2,574 citations for the 1990 book (metadata only).
limits: Not opened this session; summary from background knowledge. Critics say it is vague about how much diversity is enough.
agent_relevance: Maps onto an agent loop where a second, differently-prompted critic must be answered before a claim is accepted.

source: Kitcher (1990) The division of cognitive labor, Journal of Philosophy 87(1):5-22
finding: Decision-theory model: a community best splits scientists across rival research programmes even if some pick a programme that looks worse to them; individual and community optima differ.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session. Zollman (a09 page notes) says the Kitcher and Strevens models assume success or failure is known to all.
agent_relevance: Argues for assigning agents to different hypotheses on purpose.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic Landscapes and the Division of Cognitive Labor, Philosophy of Science 76(2)
finding: Agent-based model on a 2-D epistemic landscape (height = epistemic significance). Agents use search rules: controls, followers (move toward evidence from others) and mavericks (avoid visited sites). Reported result: populations with mavericks reach high ground faster and more fully.
numbers: Not read; I recall a large square grid and runs on landscapes of different shapes, but did not verify numbers. Crossref: about 220 citations.
limits: Not opened (publisher blocked). Alexander et al. (2015) challenge the result (next line).
agent_relevance: A direct computational model for splitting agents into follower and maverick roles.

source: Alexander, Himmelreich and Thompson (2015) Epistemic Landscapes, Optimal Search, and the Division of Cognitive Labor, Philosophy of Science 82
finding: Re-examines the Weisberg-Muldoon model. As I recall it, the finding that mavericks help depends on the follower rule used; with a better search rule the benefit of division of labor weakens or disappears.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded. Crossref: about 59 citations.
limits: Not opened (PhilSci archive blocked). My recollection should be checked before use.
agent_relevance: Warns that gains from role diversity can be artefacts of weak baseline agents.

source: Thompson (2014) Does Diversity Trump Ability? An example of the misuse of mathematics in the social sciences, Notices of the AMS 61(9)
finding: Mathematician's critique: the Hong-Page theorem is trivial or conditional on assumptions that fail for real groups, and the simulation parameters do not carry the real-world claim.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened (publisher blocked). Cited by Karge (a14) as the main criticism of rigour.
agent_relevance: Treat 'diversity trumps ability' as conditional, not general.

source: Singer (2019) Diversity, Not Randomness, Trumps Ability, Philosophy of Science 86
finding: Re-analysis of the Hong-Page simulation: diversity, not randomness, is the active ingredient. Recalled only; unverified.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened (blocked). Singer's agent-based model is the base of a15.
agent_relevance: Pick team members for diversity, not at random.

source: Grim, Singer, Bramson, McGeehan and Berger (2019) Diversity, Ability, and Expertise in Epistemic Communities, Philosophy of Science 86
finding: Simulation study of when diversity does and does not beat ability. I recall results depend on landscape structure and on how expertise is defined. Details unverified.
numbers: Not read. Crossref: about 40 citations.
limits: Not opened (blocked).
agent_relevance: Another reason to test, not assume, diversity benefits on our own tasks.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner and O'Connor (2017) In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? Philosophy of Science 84
finding: Shows the Zollman effect (sparser networks do better) depends on parameter choices; it appears mainly on hard problems and costs efficiency. Described in a13 by the review.
numbers: Not read directly; relies on the review's summary. Crossref: about 87 citations.
limits: Not opened (blocked). Counts as a boundary condition on Zollman.
agent_relevance: Do not cut sharing between agents by default.

source: Lazer and Friedman (2007) The Network Structure of Exploration and Exploitation, Administrative Science Quarterly 52
finding: NK-landscape model: in the long run, less connected groups find better solutions, while fully connected ones are faster early. Same as the review's description.
numbers: Not read; the review's one-line summary (a11) is the only source.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Staged sharing (isolated early, merged late) is a plausible scheme.

source: Kummerfeld and Zollman (2016) Conservatism and the Scientific State of Nature, BJPS 67
finding: Individual exploration beyond one's own best guess raises community success, but scientists are not paid for it, so exploration is under-supplied (free rider problem). Source here is the review (a12).
numbers: Not read directly.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Budget a fixed share of agent effort for exploration outside the leading hypothesis.

source: Wang, Wang, Athiwaratkun, Zhang and Zou (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
finding: Layered ensemble of different LLMs: each agent sees the previous layer's outputs. Beat GPT-4 Omni on AlpacaEval 2.0 using only open models, which was read as support for diversity.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0: 65.1% for MoA versus 57.5% for GPT-4 Omni; also best on MT-Bench and FLASK.
limits: Abstract read only. A later study (a28) shows the gain may come from quality, not diversity.
agent_relevance: Mixing different models is a tested design for a multi-sample agent.

source: Li, Lin, Xia and Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Direct test of diversity versus ability for LLMs. Sampling many outputs from the single best model (Self-MoA) beat mixing different models in most settings. MoA is sensitive to proposer quality, and mixing lowers average quality. Mixed models help only in some settings, such as specialist models on different tasks.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6 points over mixed MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0 (six open models, same setup as Wang et al.); +2-3 points when using the two best models; average +3.8% across MMLU, CRUX, MATH.
quote: mixing different LLMs often lowers the average quality of the models
limits: Intra-model diversity (many samples from one model) is the ingredient; supports 'ability beats cross-model diversity when quality gaps are large'. Reported by authors, not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: Important for our single agent: many samples from the strongest model may beat mixing weaker models; check quality gaps first.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Multi-agent debate with different model families beat debate among copies of one model, which beat single models, at all scales tested.
numbers: After 4 debate rounds, Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 7Bx8 + PaLM 2-M scored 91% on GSM-8K, above GPT-4, versus 82% for 3 copies of Gemini-Pro; 94% on ASDiv.
limits: Single author, small set of models, abstract read only. Conflicts in spirit with Self-MoA (a28), which used a different aggregation scheme.
agent_relevance: Supports diverse-model debate; the two results show the answer depends on task and method.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum and Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several instances of a model propose and criticise answers over rounds; improves maths, strategy and factual accuracy, reducing hallucination. Base design used by Hegazy.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures recorded here.
limits: Instances are copies of the same model, so this tests mutual criticism more than diversity.
agent_relevance: Mutual criticism with an uptake rule echoes Longino's norms.
